idiom_name: unexported struct field + checked methods in one package; os.Root for path-confined resources
implementation_notes: Go's encapsulation is package-scoped: 'An identifier is exported if ... the first character of the identifier's name is a Unicode uppercase letter ... and the identifier is declared in the package block or it is a field name or method name. All other identifiers are not exported', so the local realization is a guard type in its own package with an unexported resource field and exported methods that consult the policy before touching the resource - code in another package cannot even name the field, and the guard can be returned as a small consumer-side interface so callers never see the concrete resource. Inside the same package there is no protection, and reflect/unsafe step around the type system ('unsafe ... contains operations that step around the type safety of Go programs'; reflect cannot set unexported fields), so the package boundary is the real enclosure and should be kept minimal. For filesystem resources the standard library now provides the owning object itself: os.Root's 'methods on Root can only access files and directories beneath a root directory', with documented TOCTOU caveats for symlink validation and Unix metadata operations.
pitfalls: The boundary is the package, not the object: any code in the same package (including files added later) reads v.store directly, so the guard's package must stay minimal and hold no other functionality.

unsafe steps around the type system and reflection reads unexported fields (though it cannot set them); a struct value copied with = copies the resource reference, so never return the concrete guard struct when only its interface is meant to be used.

An interface is not an enclosure: embedding the resource type promotes its methods and re-exposes them, returning the resource as any (or through reflection) defeats the guard, and a broad interface handed to callers can be type-asserted back to the concrete type.

os.Root confines paths but documents races: symlink validation can be TOCTOU on some platforms and Chmod/Chown/Chtimes are 'vulnerable to a race condition' on Unix, so path confinement is not the same as descriptor ownership.

variants.name: os.Root confined handle (stdlib owning object)
variants.implementation_notes: For file trees the standard library supplies the owning object: 'Methods on Root can only access files and directories beneath a root directory. If any component of a file name passed to a method of Root references a location outside the root, the method returns an error.' Construct one with os.OpenRoot(dir) and hand clients the Root - they can only address paths beneath it, and the Root's own methods reject permission bits outside 0o777 and validate names like fs.FS. This is the strongest in-language realization available because the confinement lives in the runtime library rather than in package hygiene. Read the caveats before relying on it: symlink validation 'is vulnerable to TOCTOU attacks' on some targets and Unix Chmod/Chown/Chtimes are documented as racy, so for hostile filesystem races fall back to openat2-style kernel guarantees.
pitfalls: Root confines paths, not identity: it has no notion of which caller may read what, so it is the ownership half of the pattern and still needs a policy check (or per-tenant roots) in front of it.
Documented races remain (symlink validation TOCTOU on some platforms, Unix Chmod/Chown/Chtimes): confinement of names does not equal atomic mediation of the underlying inode.
A Root is a handle to a directory, not to a file: handing out a *os.File opened through it passes the file outside the root's future control, exactly like a leaked descriptor in C.
